messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Firefighter
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 40

# Vignette: The Smoke He Cannot Leave Behind

Minh is a 77-year-old Vietnamese man who has spent the last thirty years working as a firefighter in a mid-sized American city — a career he chose, his wife believes, because he already knew how to walk toward fire. What she means, though she says it gently, is that he learned long before he ever held a hose.

He was nineteen years old when the bombing reached his village in the Mekong Delta. It was 1967, and he had been helping his father repair the roof of their family home when the sky changed. He remembers the sound first — not the explosion itself, but the silence just before it, the way the birds stopped. Then the world came apart. Three neighbors were killed within sight of him. A woman he had known since childhood was carried past him in pieces. He spent the following hours pulling debris away from the collapsed wall of a nearby house with his bare hands, finding a child alive and two adults who were not. He does not talk about what the adults looked like. He has never talked about that.

He immigrated to the United States in 1979, married his wife Linh two years later, and built what he describes as a good life. His children are grown. He has grandchildren who call him on weekends. He goes to temple. On the surface, the decades have been kind.

But Minh does not sleep well. He has not slept well in fifty years, though he frames this as simply the way he is built — a man who wakes early, who sits in the kitchen before dawn with tea he does not taste. What he does not say easily is that most mornings he wakes from the same compressed, airless dream: he is under something heavy and cannot move, and there is a sound that is not quite crying. He lies still afterward, heart slamming, and waits for the feeling to pass. Sometimes it takes an hour.

At work — even now, in a reduced capacity as a trainer and mentor for younger firefighters — certain things reach him without warning. The smell of burning wood is the worst. There is a particular quality to structural fire smoke, dense and low, that moves through him like a key turning in a lock he cannot see. On two occasions in the past year he has had to step outside during training exercises, telling his colleagues he needed air, standing alone in the parking lot until his hands stopped shaking. He has not told anyone what actually happens in those moments: that he is briefly, completely, back in 1967, and the parking lot does not exist.

He is hypervigilant in ways he has normalized entirely. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He monitors exits. When his grandchildren play loudly and a door slams, his body responds before his mind does — a full-system alert that he dampens quickly, ashamed of it. Linh has learned not to touch him from behind.

What brings him in now is not any single crisis but a kind of accumulated weight. His youngest grandchild recently did a school project on the Vietnam War and asked him questions he could not answer — not because he did not know, but because his throat closed. He sat with the child's poster on the kitchen table afterward for a long time, looking at photographs he recognized from the inside, and something shifted. He tells his therapist, quietly, that he thinks he has been carrying something he does not know how to put down. He is not sure, after all this time, that he deserves to put it down.

He is a man who has spent his adult life running into burning buildings, and he will tell you without irony that this has never frightened him the way that morning in 1967 still does — because at least in a fire, he knows what he is supposed to do.
